sources.:question/problem: Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=x+y$ along the curve $C$ parametrized by $r(t)=⟨t,\,1+t⟩$ for $t\in [0,1].$
sources.:question/worked-solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Since $r(t)=⟨t,\,1+t⟩,$ then along the curve we have $x=t$ and $y=1+t.$    

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+t)j \\  & =\,i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+1} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x+y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =t+(1+t)=2t+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(2t+1)\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}2t+1\,\text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{2}{[{t}^{2}+t]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\sqrt{2}(1+1-0) \\  & =2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

sources.:question/problem:
Evaluate the integral $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}(2{x}^{2}-16)\,\text{d}s,
$$ where $C$ is the curve parametrized by $r(t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j$ for $0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{4}.$
sources.:question/worked-solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Since $r(t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,$ then along the curve we have $x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ and $y=4\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$  

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16{sin}^{2}⁡t+16{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{16({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{16} \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if $f(x,y)=2{x}^{2}-16$, then we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}-16 \\  & =16(2{cos}^{2}⁡t-1) \\  & =16\operatorname{cos}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(2{x}^{2}-16)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}16\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\cdot 4\,\text{d}t \\  & =64{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,\text{d}t \\  & =64{[\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t]}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =32[\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)-\operatorname{sin}⁡0] \\  & =32(1-0) \\  & =32.\end{aligned}
$$

sources.:question/problem:
Evaluate the integral $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}s,
$$ where $C$ is the curve parametrized by $r(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j$ for $0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{4}.$
sources.:question/worked-solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Since $r(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,$ then along the curve we have $x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ and $y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$  

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡t+4{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{4({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if $f(x,y)={y}^{2}$, then we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & ={(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}=4{sin}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}4{sin}^{2}⁡t\cdot 2\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =8{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =8{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\left(\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}{2}\right)\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)\text{d}t \\  & =4{[t-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡2t}{2}]}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =4[(\frac{\pi }{4}-\frac{1}{2})-0] \\  & =\pi -2.\end{aligned}
$$

sources.:question/problem: Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{1}{y-x}$ along the curve $C$ parametrized by $r(t)=⟨t,\,t-4⟩$ for $t\in [0,4].$
sources.:question/worked-solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Since $r(t)=⟨t,\,t-4⟩,$ then along the curve we have $x=t$ and $y=t-4.$     

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-4)j \\  & =i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+1} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\frac{1}{y-x}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{1}{t-(4-t)}=-\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{4}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}-\frac{1}{4}\cdot \sqrt{2}\,\cdot \,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}{\int }_{0}^{4}\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}t\,{|}_{0}^{4} \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}\cdot (4-0) \\  & =-\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

sources.:question/problem:
Evaluate the integral $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}({x}^{3}-2{y}^{3})\,\text{d}s,
$$ where $C$ is the curve parametrized by $r(t)=4{t}^{2}\,i+3{t}^{2}\,j$ for $0\le t\le 1.$
sources.:question/worked-solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Since $r(t)=4{t}^{2}\,i+3{t}^{2}\,j,$ then along the curve we have $x=4{t}^{2}$ and $y=3{t}^{2}.$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4{t}^{2})i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2})j \\  & =8t\,i+6t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(8t)^{2}+(6t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{64{t}^{2}+36{t}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{100{t}^{2}} \\  & =10|t| \\  & =10t.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $|t|=t$ since $t>0$ along the path of $C.$ 

Now, if $f(x,y)={x}^{3}-2{y}^{3}$, then we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & ={(4{t}^{2})}^{3}-2{(3{t}^{2})}^{3} \\  & ={4}^{3}{t}^{6}-2\cdot {3}^{3}{t}^{6} \\  & =64{t}^{6}-54{t}^{6} \\  & =10{t}^{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{3}-{y}^{3})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}10{t}^{6}\cdot 10t\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =100{\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{7}\,\text{d}t \\  & =100\cdot \frac{{t}^{8}}{8}\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =100[\frac{{1}^{8}}{8}+\frac{{0}^{8}}{8}] \\  & =100\cdot \frac{1}{8} \\  & =12.5.\end{aligned}
$$

exemplars.:question/problem:
Evaluate the line integral of $f(x,y)=x+y$ along the curve $C$ parametrized by

$$
\mathbf r(t)=\langle 2t,1+2t\rangle,\qquad 0\le t\le 1.
$$
exemplars.:question/worked-solution:
For a scalar line integral with respect to arc length, use

$$
\int_C f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=\int_a^b f(\mathbf r(t))\,\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Along the curve, $x=2t$ and $y=1+2t$. Differentiate the path and compute its speed:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf r'(t)&=\langle 2,2\rangle,\\
\|\mathbf r'(t)\|&=\sqrt{2^2+2^2}=2\sqrt{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute the coordinates into the scalar function:

$$
f(\mathbf r(t))=2t+(1+2t)=1+4t.
$$

Multiply by the speed before integrating:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_C (x+y)\,\mathrm{d}s
&=\int_0^1 (1+4t)\,2\sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{d}t\\
&=2\sqrt{2}\left[t+2t^2\right]_0^1\\
&=2\sqrt{2}(1+2)=6\sqrt{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

exemplars.:question/problem:
Evaluate the integral

$$
\int_C y^2\,\mathrm{d}s,
$$

where $C$ is parametrized by

$$
\mathbf r(t)=\langle 2\cos t,2\sin t\rangle,\qquad 0\le t\le \frac{\pi}{2}.
$$
exemplars.:question/worked-solution:
For a scalar line integral with respect to arc length, use

$$
\int_C f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=\int_a^b f(\mathbf r(t))\,\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

The path is the quarter circle of radius $2$ shown below.

![Quarter circle of radius 2 from (2,0) to (0,2), traversed counterclockwise.](images/6d/6d933c280ebb530aefaadc1b5ef927e39603635960348255045c138ee9bab366.png)

Along the curve, $x=2\cos t$ and $y=2\sin t$. Compute

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf r'(t)&=\langle -2\sin t,2\cos t\rangle,\\
\|\mathbf r'(t)\|&=\sqrt{4\sin^2t+4\cos^2t}=2,\\
f(\mathbf r(t))&=(2\sin t)^2=4\sin^2t.
\end{aligned}
$$

The integral involves $\sin^2t$, so use the identity $\sin^2t=(1-\cos 2t)/2$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_C y^2\,\mathrm{d}s
&=8\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^2t\,\mathrm{d}t\\
&=4\int_0^{\pi/2}(1-\cos 2t)\,\mathrm{d}t\\
&=4\left[t-\frac{\sin 2t}{2}\right]_0^{\pi/2}\\
&=4\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-0\right)=2\pi.
\end{aligned}
$$

exemplars.:question/problem:
Evaluate the integral

$$
\int_C (x^2+y^2-2)\,\mathrm{d}s,
$$

where $C$ is parametrized by

$$
\mathbf r(t)=\langle 2(\cos t+t\sin t),2(\sin t-t\cos t)\rangle.
$$

for $0\le t\le 1$.
exemplars.:question/worked-solution:
For a scalar line integral with respect to arc length, use

$$
\int_C f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=\int_a^b f(\mathbf r(t))\,\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Use the product rule in both components. The terms without a factor of $t$ cancel:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x'(t)&=2(-\sin t+\sin t+t\cos t)=2t\cos t,\\
y'(t)&=2(\cos t-\cos t+t\sin t)=2t\sin t,\\
\|\mathbf r'(t)\|&=\sqrt{4t^2\cos^2t+4t^2\sin^2t}\\
&=2|t|=2t.
\end{aligned}
$$

Here $|t|=t$ because $0\le t\le 1$. The speed is zero only at the starting endpoint.

Next, substitute both coordinates. Expanding the squares cancels the mixed terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x(t)^2+y(t)^2
&=4\bigl[(\cos t+t\sin t)^2+(\sin t-t\cos t)^2\bigr]\\
&=4\bigl[\cos^2t+2t\sin t\cos t+t^2\sin^2t\\
&\qquad+\sin^2t-2t\sin t\cos t+t^2\cos^2t\bigr]\\
&=4(1+t^2).
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus $f(\mathbf r(t))=4(1+t^2)-2=2+4t^2$. Multiply this by the variable speed and integrate each term:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_C (x^2+y^2-2)\,\mathrm{d}s
&=\int_0^1 (2+4t^2)\,2t\,\mathrm{d}t\\
&=\int_0^1 (4t+8t^3)\,\mathrm{d}t\\
&=\left[2t^2+2t^4\right]_0^1\\
&=2+2=4.
\end{aligned}
$$
